entities.summary:
Nicolas de Pellevé (1518–1594) emerged as a formidable French cardinal and archbishop, a central architect and ardent proponent of the ultra-Catholic faction during the tumultuous French Wars of Religion (1562-1598). His career, spanning decades of intense religious and political strife in Western Europe, saw him rise through the ecclesiastical ranks to become Archbishop of Sens (1562), then Reims (1591), and finally a Cardinal (1570). Pellevé's significance lies in his unwavering allegiance to the Holy See and the powerful Guise family, positioning him as a vocal opponent of both Huguenot Protestantism and the moderate Catholic policies of King Henry III, ultimately championing the hardline stance of the Catholic League.

Throughout his tenure, Pellevé was deeply involved in the machinations of the French court and the broader European Catholic revival. As a trusted advisor to Catherine de' Medici and later a staunch supporter of the Guises, he played a crucial role in shaping royal policy, particularly regarding the suppression of Protestantism. His influence was evident in the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572), which, while not directly orchestrated by him, reflected the violent anti-Huguenot sentiment he espoused. He actively participated in the States-General of Blois (1576), advocating for the eradication of Protestantism in France and aligning himself with the nascent Catholic League, which sought to prevent a Protestant (Henry of Navarre) from ascending to the throne.
